Vendredi soir, le soleil se couche lente: Friday evening, the sun slowly sets on the horizon. It is 9 p.m., and shops are closing their doors. Friends gather in restaurants and cafés to celebrate the weekend. Meanwhile, in a room at the Forum Jeunesse Saint Michel, something remarkable is taking shape. The creaking door opens, and a symphony of chaâbi drifts down the stairs. Here, Algiers resounds. Here, Algiers lives. The notes, like heart-rending laments, evoke a nostalgic beauty.
La Converse s’est immiscée dans l’intimi: La Converse slipped into the intimate world of the Orchestre Chaâbi de Montréal (OCM) during its rehearsals, behind-the-scenes conversations and performances, in order to better understand the very particular devotion that brings 20 people together every week. The word “chaâbi,” which refers to a true musical jewel from Algiers, comes from the Arabic word chaab, which means “people”. Chaâbi is therefore tied to the notion of “popular” in Arabic.

Dans l’enceinte de ces cafés, l’histoire: Within the walls of these cafés, history is forged, carried by passionate souls, including Mourad Taleb, a former maestro, alongside Nassim Gadouch and Lamine Djanki, who floated the idea of creating a non-profit chaâbi orchestra. The goal is to celebrate Maghrebi diversity, with particular attention to Algeria. “We want to bring the community together,” says Sofiane Benyahia, president of the OCM.
Depuis 2017, la vingtaine de musiciens e: Since 2017, the Orchestre Chaâbi de Montréal’s some twenty musicians and choristers have gathered every Friday night. From 9 p.m. to midnight, time fades away. The musicians surrender to the musical alchemy and strive to perfect their art.
Karima Bougherara, l’une des choristes,: Karima Bougherara, one of the choristers, has lived in Quebec since 2007. She stresses the importance of making Algerian music shine in Quebec’s artistic landscape. “It’s essential that we be seen for our true worth. We have a history, a culture, a richness. We’re not just immigrants who came here to work; we also have knowledge,” says the former talent agent. She adds: “The media never portray Algeria from this angle, never show that we are joyful, creative, sensitive people. They talk about us as a country marked by civil war and violence.”
À l’OCM, elle remplit ce qu’elle considè: At the OCM, she fulfills what she considers to be a “duty.” “And I do it with pleasure, the pleasure of sharing this music, (…) especially with young people, particularly those of the diaspora who don’t easily have access to it.” Sofiane chimes in: “When our kids go to school, they learn neither their history, nor their language, nor their culture. When my kids ask me, ‘Dad, what is the Algerian war? Why are we here?’ it kills me, it breaks my heart!”
Redouane, lui aussi père de famille, est: Redouane, also a father, shares this view. “Through chaâbi, we want to encourage young people to learn their language, that heart that makes culture beat.” He even created a music school to ease the effects of cultural uprooting among young people of Algerian origin. “His initiative is precious. I didn’t have anything like it growing up in Canada. Having a place where your mother tongue is spoken, where your customs are appreciated and your history is valued is vital to building who you are,” says Ali.
Lamine Djanki, surnommé « l’Encyclopédie: Lamine Djanki, nicknamed “the Encyclopedia” by his OCM companions, takes us to the heart of chaâbi’s history. “Chaâbi is the fruit of the fusion of <l1>Arab-Andalusian</l1> classical music and <l2>melhoun</l2>, which carries Maghrebi dialectal poetry,” he explains. The subjects chaâbi addresses are fundamental shared experiences: friendship and love, for example.
Cette « musique du peuple » est venue co: This “music of the people” came to fill a void: “In the 19th century, classical Arab-Andalusian music, like the <l1>nouba</l1>, reigned supreme in royal courts and was reserved for an enlightened elite. Its theoretical complexity and its use of literary Arabic made it inaccessible to the vast majority of people. There was also <l2>medh</l2>, that is, songs of praise of a religious and spiritual nature. These musical genres seemed either too hermetic or too solemn, lacking the rhythm and cadence that could have evoked the common experiences and deep lived reality of the people,” explains Lamine.
Au fil du temps, les cheikhs (des maître: Over time, the cheikhs (musical masters) and their disciples dared to innovate and revolutionized the Algerian musical landscape. The one who changed the course of the country’s musical history is undeniably El Hadj M’Hamed El Anka, the musician adds.
El Anka, né en 1907, est une figure inco: El Anka, born in 1907, is an essential figure in Algerian music. This alchemist of sound drew his inspiration from the artistic currents that nourish Algerian musical life, steeping himself in songs of praise in Tamazight, Kabyle <l1>Achewiq</l1> and the bewitching melodies of Constantine’s <l2>malouf </l2>. “He even innovated in classical orchestration, turning the guitar into a mandolin, swapping the oud (lute) for the banjo-guitar and replacing the kamanja (Arab violin) with the viola,” marvels our interviewee.
« L’histoire du chaâbi est une chaîne, u: “The history of chaâbi is a chain, a continuity. It is passed from cheikh to cheikh, from master to master,” adds Lamine, forming a ring with his fingers, a symbol of this transmission. Indeed, people learn without sheet music, and everything rests on oral transmission. “Everything is passed on by ear, everything is kept in memory. Chaâbi is alive. It lives in us. Memory plays an essential role, both historically and in terms of musical technique,” says Ali with emotion.
Ce fil invisible, qui tisse l’histoire d: This invisible thread, which weaves the history of chaâbi, reaches all the way to Montréal. As Redouane leads the orchestra with an expert hand, Lamine shares the following with pride: “Our artistic director, Redouane, is a true prodigy of Algerian music. He joined the Algerian Symphony Orchestra at the age of six, showing his exceptional talent very early.” Lamine then adds: “Redouane is the only one with formal training in music. He was trained by Abdeslam Darouache, a direct disciple of the illustrious Hadj El Anka himself!” Break time arrives; the musicians slip away briefly to stretch their tired legs and enjoy mint tea and delicious Algerian pastries that melt in the mouth.
Ali, Sofiane et Redouane témoignent de l: Ali, Sofiane and Redouane speak to Lamine’s humility and praise his essential role as keeper of chaâbi’s history. “He is an undisputed reference for chaâbi, here as in Algeria. He embodies a living memory,” says Ali. In an art form where words are not fixed on paper, Lamine indeed applies himself with disarming precision and passion to authenticating the lyrics and bringing this timeless music to life.
L’humilité est une vertu profondément an: Humility is a virtue deeply rooted in this musical brotherhood. Here, no one boasts of their own merits, but everyone is ready to heap praise on those of their comrades.

C’est à l’École Ladjrafi Musique d’Algér: It is at the École Ladjrafi Musique d’Algérie et Arts (ELMAA), located in Montréal’s Saint-Léonard neighbourhood, that we meet OCM members for the second time.
Nous pénétrons dans une pièce aux murs o: We step into a room whose walls are adorned with zellige, a meticulously crafted Maghrebi ornamental mosaic. An oriental rug spreads its colours beneath lanterns with golden arabesques. Two hanging paintings depict a fantasia, a Maghrebi equestrian tradition.
Mohamed Zikara, un jeune homme de 33 ans: Mohamed Zikara, a 33-year-old man, picks up his mandola-guitar to offer us an istikhbar, a musical improvisation. “I crossed your doors with no plan, simply to see you, or to see the one who once saw you. Passion quenched my thirst with a glass of pure love. May that same passion quench yours.”*
Redouane, Sofiane, Mohamed et Ali discut: Redouane, Sofiane, Mohamed and Ali talk around a table laden with honey-soaked griwech , a traditional pastry. These four men took different migration paths, but one immigration experience unites them: that of exile.
Dès l’adolescence, Ali s’est senti attir: From adolescence, Ali felt drawn to Algerian music. “It’s this feeling of exile (…) that pushed me to reconnect with my community. Fifteen years later, I find myself on stage alongside great musicians who have become my friends,” he says, moved.
Mohamed enchaîne : « Je suis tombé sur l: Mohamed follows up: “I came across the Orchestre Chaâbi’s video by chance. I told myself I had to do everything I could to join this team,” he says with a joyful laugh. “In fact, it’s one of the main reasons I moved from Gatineau to Montréal.”
Le Montréalais de fraîche date poursuit: The new Montrealer continues: “For me, the difference between playing chaâbi in Montréal and in Algiers is that now I live the lyrics. Chaâbi often deals with the theme of exile, but before, I sang without really understanding that homesickness. Now we truly feel the words, we understand them. We’re carried by this feeling of nostalgia, because we are very far from our country, and that distance only grows with time.”
Sofiane renchérit : « Je me rappelle qua: Sofiane adds: “I remember when I was young, I sang ‘Ya rayah’ (O you who leave) without really dwelling on its depth. We used to say among ourselves that it was a song for emigrants. But now we’re in it, we are the rayah, the ones who left. Before, it was just a song, but now it’s my own life it’s talking about.”
« Quand nous partageons ces musiques-là: “When we share this music with the audience and thousands of spectators sing the chorus with us, it’s the feeling of saudade [that comes through], the blues, the spleen, that indescribable feeling that touches every sensitive soul,” says Alilou.
Pour Redouane, la scène permet de se res: For Redouane, the stage is a way to recharge. His friend Sofiane even calls it a form of therapy. “Instead of seeing a therapist, we pick up our instruments and sing. Whether it’s among friends, within the orchestra or in front of an audience, this feeling is powerful and liberating.”
En exil, dans cette situation où l’on se: In exile, in this situation of finding yourself between two worlds, music becomes a universal language. It transcends borders and soothes torment. It offers refuge, self-expression and a connection with others.

Le 22 juin 2023, les Jardins Gamelin se: On June 22, 2023, the Jardins Gamelin are transformed into a time capsule. On this dance floor, time seems suspended, and chaâbi’s contagious energy sweeps every spectator into a joyful trance. Faces light up, smiles widen, the atmosphere turns electric. The musicians’ virtuosity shows in every note.
l’OCM en concert au Jardins Gamelin: The OCM in concert at the Jardins Gamelin
La musique s’intensifie, le public se la: The music intensifies, and the audience lets itself be carried away by the bewitching cadence. Graceful gestures and rhythmic steps intertwine. Eyes meet, hands reach out to invite new partners to join the dance. Ululations, cries of joy and excitement, ring through the air, adding a touch of euphoria and celebration.
Rachid, un Algérien de 42 ans, ne cesse: Rachid, a 42-year-old Algerian, doesn’t stop dancing. No matter the song, he knows all the words. “We’re here today because the OCM makes us vibrate at every show. It brings the community together, it shows our beautiful culture to this beautiful country, Canada,” he says enthusiastically. Settled here for about ten years, this Canadian citizen looks at those around him and adds: “We really feel like we’re in our houma, our neighbourhood; we feel like we’re in Algiers, despite the thousands of kilometres. There was an older man I was dancing with; he was wearing a typically Algiers outfit called bleu shanghai. It does the soul good.”
Les générations se mélangent. Les grands: Generations mix. Grandparents, parents and relatives guide the children through the dances, languages and sensations. Here, at the Jardins Gamelin, the dance floor becomes a space of cultural exchange among the Algerian, Maghrebi and Québécois communities.
« En regardant la foule, je me rends com: “Looking at the crowd, I realize it’s not only Maghrebis who are enjoying this. There are so many other people who appreciate this music. It makes me proud to see it resonate so many kilometres from its cradle,” exclaims Remy. Having grown up in Quebec, he finds the OCM’s volunteer work necessary. “I’m really happy to see so many kids, so many young people, who support the orchestra and contribute to the fulfillment of its mission,” the young man adds.
Mohamed Zikara, héritier spirituel du lé: Mohamed Zikara, spiritual heir of the legendary singer El Hachemi Guerouabi, conveys with intensity all the emotion and nostalgia of the song Allo Allo – Wahdani Gharib (Allo Allo – Lonely Stranger). Originally from Belcourt, a neighbourhood of Algiers, Mohamed evokes homesickness. His voice is tinged with saudade. He speaks of the absence of his beloved neighbourhood. “I miss you too much / Belcourt, how great its worth / where I left the scent of my parents / and my loved ones and neighbours / My loved ones and my people and my neighbours.”1 In front of him, the spectators sing “Djazaïr zinet el bouldan ” (Algeria, the most beautiful of countries) at every chorus.
Puis, des notes de derbouka résonnent et: Then the notes of a darbuka ring out and announce the start of the famous song Ya Rayah. If some spectators had resisted dancing earlier, now they are all gathered; the floor is packed. The excitement grows as the first words ring out: “O you who leave, wherever you travel, you leave, you wear yourself out, and you will end up coming back. ”
Le public, ému, chante la chanson à l’un: The moved audience sings the song in unison. Voices blend into a powerful chorus, while cries of joy, ululations, can be heard all around. The dance steps become slower and charged with emotion. Arms link, faces hide, tears fall.
<em>Ya Rayah </em>évoque le déchirement: Ya Rayah evokes the heartbreak of exile, nostalgia for the native land and the hope of return. The words echo in everyone’s heart, recalling the memories, hopes and dreams left behind.
Khadija, elle, a quitté Bejaïa pour le C: Khadija left Bejaïa for Canada barely a year ago. “After my workday, I came straight here with my two daughters. I feel an intense nostalgia for my country, which I miss enormously. Even though I don’t know anyone here, in this crowd, I feel like I’m with family.” For her too, passing Algerian culture on to her children is paramount. “I don’t want them to lose their culture. That’s why I’ll keep bringing them to events like this,” says this new Quebecer proudly.
L’OCM a créé une communion musicale, où: The OCM has created a musical communion, where every chorus is at once a prayer, a plea and a good time. Here, it is Montréal that resounds. The concert is coming to an end, and the crowd of about 3,000 people disperses. One thing is certain with the Orchestre Chaâbi de Montréal: “O you who leave, wherever you travel, you leave, you wear yourself out, and you will end up coming back.”

Dans les cafés du Petit Maghreb, à Montr: In the cafés of Montréal’s Petit Maghreb, devoted fans of chaâbi and Algerian music gather for informal get-togethers. Ali Idres, a 27-year-old Algerian and spokesperson for the OCM, explains: “The regulars, the artists and the music lovers knew that Friday night at Café Oasis was chaâbi night. So we get together with our instruments and our songs, and we all play together. It’s a way to forget exile and to find again, even if just for a moment, the scent of the bled [the homeland].”
